problem: Object-goal navigation models assume a fixed set of object categories and full data access; when new categories arrive sequentially they suffer catastrophic forgetting (representation drift in the encoder, policy degradation in the decoder), and naive raw-trajectory replay is memory-heavy, privacy-sensitive and redundant.
motivation: Open-world agents must keep learning new goal categories without retraining from scratch. Continual learning for long-horizon multimodal embodied navigation had not been studied, and no benchmark existed. Fine-tuning drops old-category SR by about 40% by the last stage.
key_idea: Mitigate forgetting with a dual path, feature distillation on the multimodal encoder plus replay of stored deep features to the action decoder, where the stored features are only LOF-selected outlier keyframes.
insight: Both paths matter and are complementary: removing KD drops average SR by about 22 points on HM3D and 16 on MP3D, and removing feature replay drops it by about 12 and 10. Replaying deep features of outlier keyframes (decision points, near targets) at half length beats uniform sampling by about 3.65 SR on HM3D and 3.2 on MP3D, and even beats full raw-trajectory replay. Fully freezing the encoder hurts, while fine-tuning the projectors under consistency regularization works better.
method: Continual-ObjectNav benchmark: 4 sequential stages with disjoint goal categories on HM3D (6 categories) and MP3D (21 categories), using Habitat-Web/PIRL human demos. After each stage the agent is evaluated on all categories seen so far, reporting Avg and Last SR/SPL, across RNN, Transformer, BEV and LLM (Qwen2-0.5B) policies.
Feature distillation (L_KD): squared L2 between frozen previous-stage encoder features and current encoder features on the same observations, keeping the multimodal representation consistent.
Feature replay (L_FR): replays stored per-frame features with action labels through the current action decoder, using inflection-weighted cross-entropy (gamma=3.48), to keep the policy consistent.

Adaptive experience selection: encode RGB frames with CLIP, compute LOF (cosine distance) over each trajectory, and keep frames with LOF>1 as keyframes. Their features f_k(o_t) and actions go into a feature buffer, with p=80 trajectories per category and about 50% of frames kept.
Overall objective: L = L_curr (behavior cloning with inflection weighting) + 5*L_KD + 5*L_FR. Frozen CLIP-RN50 RGB and depth ResNet-50 encoders, with projectors fine-tuned.

setting.backbone: CLIP-ResNet50 + depth ResNet-50 encoders (frozen) with projectors; action decoders LSTM / 4-layer Transformer / BEV-Transformer / Qwen2-0.5B, trained sequentially
setting.training_data: Habitat-Web / PIRL human demonstration trajectories: HM3D 75,488 and MP3D 59,604, split into 4 category stages
setting.observation: egocentric RGB-D + pose + previous action + object goal name
setting.action_space: discrete low-level: move_forward, turn_left, turn_right, look_up, look_down, stop
setting.privileged: none at test time (replay buffer of stored features from earlier stages during training)

numbers.extra: continual 4-stage setting, Avg over stages / Last stage; p=80 feature buffer, 50% keyframes

numbers_note: Split is the official ObjectNav validation split (2,000 HM3D / 2,195 MP3D episodes), reported under the continual protocol. Metrics are Avg over stages and Last stage, so keys are SR_avg/SR_last etc. Some ablation and zero-shot (VLFM) comparisons appear only in figures.
results: C-Nav beats all continual baselines (Finetuning, LoRA, LwF, Merge, data replay) on all four architectures and both datasets. Against the strongest baseline, full-trajectory data replay, it gains an average SR of 3.35 on MP3D and 2.75 on HM3D with lower storage. Example: HM3D-Bev Last SR is 46.5 versus 44.2 for DP.
limitations: Simulation only (Habitat); no real-robot validation, and sensor noise and lighting changes are untested
Storage still grows linearly with the number of tasks
Only a few categories per stage and 4 stages; categories are disjoint and the LLM decoder is small (0.5B)
